anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.text:
## (1) First message

The framing holds as far as the gathered evidence reaches. I checked the gather draft's trace of the reports page, which renders a table and has no export action. I also checked the table's column definitions and `src/export/csv.ts`, which the draft cites as already reusing those definitions, and the paging path, which the draft says supports the 10k-row target. Implementing the ask through that existing serializer is not a band-aid and creates no second path. I had no tool access in this pass, so I could not open primary code. The premises below are marked to match.

**Premises**

- **Supported by the draft only.** The draft says the column definitions and the existing CSV serializer already support export, and that `src/export/csv.ts` reuses the table's column definitions. I have not confirmed this in primary code, so it stays unverified until the file is read during spec writing.
- **Unverified.** The draft says paging supports the 10k-row target. The ticket's third row requires a 10k-row export to finish in under 60s, so this matters. Checking it needs two things that are not named in the draft, the repo, or the ticket:
  - a 10k-row report fixture or seed
  - a timing harness

  I found neither, so this is an unverified implicit dependency. The spec will carry it into `## Problem` and Open Questions, and the design will need to add both.
- **Disproved or corrected.** None.

**Assumptions**

- The ticket groups its rows by repo. The `acme/widgets` group matches this repo, per overrides `repo: acme/widgets`, so its three rows are `in-scope`.
- The `acme/mailer` row, "Exports are emailed to the requesting user", is `elsewhere: acme/mailer`. It is delivered by that repo, and this spec creates no work for it.

Where on the reports page should the Export CSV button appear?
A) Beside the report title
B) In the table toolbar, above the column headers
C) In a page-level actions menu
other - name it
Recommendation: A - it is visible without any extra click and does not compete with table controls, and the page has no actions menu to extend.

## (2) Approaches message

Before the approaches, one implicit dependency is still open. Verifying the third row, a 10k-row export in under 60s, needs a 10k-row report fixture and a timing harness. I looked for both in the draft, the ticket, and the overrides, and none names either. The dependency is recorded as not checkable, and the chosen approach must add both.

The two options differ on one point: where the full report is assembled into CSV. It can be built in the page from existing paging, or streamed from a new server endpoint. Both put the button beside the report title, as you answered. Both export the visible table columns in table order, which the spec will write as a Design clause for the row "every column shown in the table".

**A) Reuse-only: page-driven export through the existing serializer (recommended).**
- The new Export CSV button walks the existing paging until every row is fetched.
- It passes the rows and the visible column definitions, in table order, to `src/export/csv.ts`.
- It triggers a download in the browser.

The serializer already consumes those definitions, so the only change to it is a column-subset/order parameter if it does not already accept one. Other callers keep the default.

The trade-offs:
- The whole report sits in browser memory.
- The 60s target depends on page size and round trips, which is still unmeasured.

Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title; export handler that iterates existing paging; optional visible-columns/order parameter on the `src/export/csv.ts` serializer; 10k-row fixture; timing test for the 60s row; tests for button presence and column parity.
Pattern: follows `src/export/csv.ts`'s existing reuse of the table column definitions, with one data path and one serializer.

**B) Drop the browser-assembly assumption: a server-side streaming endpoint.**
- A new endpoint runs the report query in pages and streams CSV from the same serializer.
- The button links to that endpoint.

This handles memory and speed better at 10k rows and beyond. It also gives `acme/mailer` an obvious server hook later. However, it adds a route and a second read path beside the paging the table already uses, without any measured need for them.

Removes: none
Adds: export endpoint and route; server-side paging loop; serializer call on the server; Export CSV button linking to the endpoint; 10k-row fixture; timing test; endpoint tests.
Pattern: cuts across the single paging read path the reports table owns by adding a parallel query path. It is justified only if paging cannot meet the target.

I recommend A: it meets all three in-scope rows with no new construct. I would switch to B if the 10k-row timing test shows page-driven export taking 60s or more, or if browser memory fails at that size.

Which approach should the spec carry?
A) Reuse the existing CSV serializer and paging from the page
B) Add a server-side streaming export endpoint
other - name it
Recommendation: A - it reuses the one serializer and paging path already shared with the table, and the timing test decides whether B is ever needed.

github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol.text:
## 1. First message to the user

The supplied draft supports adding export to the reports page using the existing CSV serializer and paging, but I cannot complete the primary-code framing check from the supplied material alone.

The draft identifies `src/export/csv.ts` as reusing table column definitions; that supports reuse rather than a parallel column mapping. Its claim that paging supports exporting 10k rows in under 60 seconds remains unverified: no implementation trace or benchmark result was supplied, and no code lookup is available here. The design must retain that ticket requirement and verify it rather than assume paging proves it.

The ticket’s `acme/widgets` group matches the recorded repository identity. Its three rows remain in scope. The email requirement belongs to the explicitly named nonmember repository, so its disposition is `elsewhere: acme/mailer`; this does not add email delivery to this repository’s implementation.

Where should the Export CSV button appear?
A) Beside the report title.
B) In the table toolbar.
C) In the page’s actions menu.
D) Other — name it.
Recommendation: A - it makes report-level export easy to discover without presenting it as an action on selected rows.

## 2. Approaches message

**I recommend reusing the existing CSV serializer and paging**, with the button beside the report title and the visible table columns exported in table order, as recorded in your answers.

The performance premise is still unverified: the supplied draft says paging supports the 10k-row target, but no benchmark or primary-code lookup was available. Paging’s ability to retrieve the complete report—not merely the displayed page—also needs confirmation. These are verification obligations, not reasons to discard the ticket’s under-60-second requirement.

The distinguishing axis is **whether export runs directly from the page action or becomes a separate background operation**.

### A. Direct export using the existing serializer and paging — recommended

The button initiates retrieval of the complete report through the existing paging path. The export passes the visible columns, in table order, to the existing serializer rather than introducing a second column definition.

This is the minimal reuse-only option. It has the fewest moving parts and directly delivers the requested button and CSV. Its main risks are whether paging can retrieve the complete report efficiently and whether serialization and download remain responsive at 10k rows. Any shared serializer change must preserve its other callers; their identities were not supplied.

Removes: None.  
Adds: Report-title button and handler; complete-report paging orchestration; visible-column selection passed through the existing serializer contract, extending that contract only if necessary; export behavior and performance tests.  
Pattern: Follows the shared-column reuse described for `src/export/csv.ts` in the gather draft; avoids a parallel CSV column mapping.

### B. Background export with a downloadable result

This drops the assumption that clicking Export must perform all export work within the page’s active operation. The button starts a background export; the page exposes progress and a download when it finishes. The export still uses the shared serializer and visible-column ordering.

This can isolate expensive work from the page, but introduces job lifecycle, result retention, status reporting, and failure handling. No existing job infrastructure was identified in the supplied material, so its availability cannot be assumed. It also must meet the same under-60-second export requirement; background execution does not relax that contract.

Removes: None.  
Adds: Report-title button and handler; export-job boundary and worker; job status and downloadable-result interfaces; result storage and cleanup; paging and serializer integration; lifecycle, export behavior, and performance tests.  
Pattern: Preserves the shared-column contract described at `src/export/csv.ts`, but introduces an asynchronous boundary not established by the supplied repository evidence.

I would switch from A to B only if measurement or the existing paging contract shows that direct export cannot meet the required performance or keep the page usable.
